title: The restoration of Baja California’s fishing communities

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When author John Steinbeck visited Mexico’s Baja California peninsula in 1940, he marveled at the incredible biodiversity: huge schools of manta rays, beds of pearl oysters, and so many turtles that older people in the region said you could cross the sea walking on their shells. But within a couple of decades, local inhabitants had overfished the waters there. After the wild oyster beds had been decimated, locals went after shrinking populations of turtles, tuna, sharks, groupers and a dozen other species. As this trend continued, the region was seeing the collapse of target species as families moved from one basic settlement to another, chasing whatever remained of the threatened fish population. Making this situation worse, a government program, called ‘March to the Sea’, encouraged unemployed workers to become fishermen.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: To counter this trend, a few small communities began to devise ways to maintain their resources. One of them – Punta Abreojos – began to modify its approach to fishing. In the 1970s, after a few disappointing harvests, the fishermen there decided to implement practices that would bring long-term benefit instead of immediate profits. Punta Abreojos now observes a self-imposed ban. Rather than fish for abalone (a type of edible sea snail) as soon as the Mexican government allows, in January, the community waits until April, when the shellfish have put on more weight.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One key to sustainable ocean management is for a community to have more or less exclusive use of a site, as in the case of Abreojos. But it also helps if the community has a resource of high value, such as lobster or abalone. One remarkable example of a high-value resource can be seen in San Ignacio, a few miles down the coast. In 1972, according to local legend, Francisco ‘Pachico’ Mayoral was fishing in his usual spot. As fishermen did in that region, he carried an oar to bang against the boat whenever a gray whale swam too close. Gray whales, everyone thought, were dangerous creatures capable of snapping a boat in half. Before long, one swam next to his boat. For some reason, Mayoral reached out to stroke the whale’s skin and, to his surprise, the whale remained calm. In that moment a new industry was born: whale watching. By the late 1980s, Mayoral and other fishermen were guiding tourists by the dozens to see the whales.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Today, whale watching is among the most important economic activities in the region, with ecotourism lodges now dotting the shoreline. San Ignacio limits the number of vessels actively in use to around 16. In addition, fishing in the lagoon is banned during the whale watching season so the whales have some peace and quiet after giving birth to new offspring. The preservation of this natural estuary does more than keep the whales safe; it does the same for crucial nursery habitats for fish and invertebrates.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Successful marine conservation also requires visionary leaders. The case of Cabo Pulmo demonstrates this. In the mid-1980s, biologists visited Cabo Pulmo and loaned local fishermen a diving mask. What the fishermen saw alarmed them – pockmarks from their anchors and overturned coral heads everywhere. And very few fish. In the early 1990s, Mario Castro, a fisherman and diver, and Tito Mijares, a bar owner, led Cabo Pulmo’s fishermen to make a bold decision to support a marine reserve. By 1995, most fishing was forbidden in a 27-square-mile area, creating a legal no-take reserve – the only well-enforced one in the region. It’s not big but it turns out you don’t need much space to bring back an ocean community. Today, Cabo Pulmo National Park has two to three times more biomass than in 2000 and the once-poor village now has a vibrant economy based on diving tourism.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: While developing a tourism model is an excellent way to save a threatened ecosystem, not every fishing village has that opportunity. Besides, tourism doesn’t create many jobs. For conservation to work, fishermen need a way to make money while they wait for their resource to recover. And the conservation efforts need manpower. To this end, the community of El Manglito has adopted an interesting strategy. Fishermen there once freely harvested shellfish from the broad, shallow bay west of town. By 2009, very few were left. With financial support from Noroeste Sustentable, a nonprofit organization in the neighboring city of La Paz, the fishermen, many of whom were involved in poaching, turned away from this illegal activity and began managing their resources. They were paid to watch for poachers and conduct biological surveys to estimate the amount of shellfish. The first survey estimated that fewer than 100,000 shellfish were left. Today it’s more like 2.3 million.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Ultimately, for conservation to work, community cohesion and trust are essential. In rural Baja, trust in one’s neighbor can be hard to find, but it’s possible to create it. At least that’s what a conservation organization called Niparajá is working to achieve. Niparajá works on sustainable fisheries in an especially desolate region of southeastern Baja. When Niparajá started working in communities there, it didn’t focus on fishing. Instead it promoted soccer tournaments. Sponsoring these in tiny towns might seem like a waste of time and money but it slowly built trust between villages that have jealously guarded fishing grounds from each other. Next Niparajá took some fishermen to Cabo Pulmo to see the impact a fishing ban can have on ocean life. Eventually, after years of discussions, the villages decided to try conservation. Each selected a small area and agreed not to fish in it for five years. The areas are not big – the largest is just under three square miles – but it was a start.
